title: This is Us
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the story of the past seven years through "This Is Us," a song by Mark Knopfler and Emmylou Harris about contentment. Nomon traces the stress that builds after Walker's birth, Janet's chronic illness, the start of a new Dharma center, and a miserable day job, and names the fears of disappointing others and of not making sense that keep a change at bay. An old client's call comes just as Nomon reaches for the office phone to give notice. The Diamond Sutra's teaching on the separate self, studied for 21 years, finally sinks in, and Nomon ends by leading a guided mindfulness session like the one offered to the Community of Christ at Samish Island.

sentences.text: Well, I was just thinking that it seems like we're not doing very much here.
Welcome back, John, too.
Just sitting there quietly, maybe just taking a break.
It looks like a vertical nap to people, but it's actually a pretty courageous thing to do.
I was realizing this evening that it's a pretty courageous thing to try to really face one's own life, you know what I mean?
Noticing what one is actually feeling is a courageous thing to do, so congratulations.
Thank you for doing that.
It's really inspiring.
And I seem to be on a bit of a jag of giving semi-autobiographical talks, so maybe I'm trying to do this work of facing my life also.
So tonight I wanted to do two different things.
First, I want to give a talk updating you on my adventures.
And secondly, I wanted to try just doing some mindfulness practices together.
So I think we won't have any discussion time this evening.
We'll just keep it very quiet.
Aside from me talking, you can have the whole evening being really quiet, not speaking.
A few months ago I gave a very emotional talk, which I wrapped around a Bruce Coburn song called Pacing the Cage.
And it's actually traditional in Zen to give talks based on poetry and art.
So I am trying to pioneer 21st century pop music as a Dharma talk framework.
So tonight I want to play you another song.
I've been quite engaged lately in exploring and trying to understand my emotional life and what makes me tick, and where suffering comes from, and where the end of suffering is coming from.
Somehow different songs keep popping up.

I don't listen to music all the time, but sometimes I listen to music, and different songs keep popping up and feel like they're expressing and helping me understand how I'm feeling a little better than I could otherwise.
Which is maybe one of the great gifts of music, a deep expression of human feeling.
The Bruce Coburn song was a very intense song about the depths of the dark side of human experience.
And there are copies of the talk in the library if you didn't hear it yet.
The lyrics are very interesting and complicated and say a lot about the human condition.
This one is more like a fluffy pop song.
But, oh, here it is, previous song, previous talk was in there.
Somehow this song for me expresses an important human feeling.
Something about contentment and feeling the underlying joy of all experience.
It's called This Is Us by Mark Knopfler, and it's performed by Mark Knopfler and Emmylou Harris.
*Down at the Mardi Gras.
This is us. [unclear: "In your daddy's You and the missing Lee"] Yeah, I had a little too much to drink.
Down in the sun.
Too much fun.*
Earth-shattering, somehow expressing something about contentment.
This is us.
This is it.
This is all we really need.
And yes, things don't always go perfectly.
Sometimes we have too much to drink.
Sometimes we can't remember the name of the parent at their kid's game.
We aren't perfect.
But we're alright.
We're content.
And we're connected.
And it doesn't really matter if we're married or in a relationship.
We're always in a relationship with the whole world.
Married to the world.
And we always have each other.
Anyway, as you might know from the other talk, I've been really studying darkness and stress, and feeling hemmed in.
Especially in the last three or four months, I felt really trapped.
Really crushed a little bit by my life.
At the same time, nothing was really wrong.
I was never in any imminent danger.
But I was not doing very well.
There was not much joy.
And I especially was noticing this in relationship to my work life, my day job.
But it wasn't really about my job.
My job, I think, was just a trigger, just the obvious thing.
Much more central and important was a powerful conditioned tendency to respond to any conditions that start to feel difficult with a very tight, solo, powerful effort.
With a lot of tension and a lot of intensity, and without really taking the existence of myself into account.
I was thinking back for this talk, so I'm getting to this.
I'm doing much better.
That's what I'm getting to.
Don't worry.
But I was thinking back about it, and I realized that I actually had a pretty challenging time for about the last seven years.
I was thinking about seven years because my son is seven and a half, so it's easy to track.
That's the main reason for a kid: you can actually keep track of time when you have one.
Before, in the 90s, I had no idea what happened when.
Anyway, seven years is an important number in Asia, I'm told.
In the West, we were sort of base 10-oriented.
We celebrate decades and 10th anniversaries and turning 40 or turning 50, where we celebrate or we dread it, depending on our scene.
But in Asia, apparently, they celebrate things in increments of seven.
So it might actually be that every seven years is a new chapter in our lives.
And maybe I'm starting a new chapter in my life.
I'm 43 now, so oddly enough, the chapter will go until I'm 50.
It works out both ways.
About seven years ago, as I said, our son was born.
And having a child, if you haven't done this, is a really powerful watershed.
For the first year or two, it's this enormous, wondrous, and unbelievably stressful time.
You really can't see straight for at least a year.
You're completely upside down.
And if you don't think that you are, you're just not paying attention.
Just as my wife and I were starting to come out of that, when Walker, our son, was about two and a half, my wife got sick.
We didn't realize then that she was getting sick.
But we were on a trip to Europe, so I can place a beginning.
Sometimes you can't place a beginning to things, but I can here.
I remember Janet was very tired and seemed constricted and grumpy a lot of the time.
And I remember sitting in this little apartment we rented for a few days, on the top floor of a little old building in the medieval center of a little Croatian town called Trogir.
I remember being really upset, in a lot of distress and despair.
Very powerful thoughts arose in my mind that the relationship wasn't going to last, that this was it.
That hadn't arisen in me before, so it was a little surprising and shocking.
At the same time, on that particular trip, Walker suddenly stopped taking naps, which he had been taking until the week before.
That was a built-in 90-minute break from his intensity.
He's a pretty intense little guy, and we counted on it.

So in the middle of this trip, there was something up with Janet, or was it something with me, and Walker wasn't taking naps, and Walker was in this mode where all he wanted to do was play with the little toys he brought along.
He wouldn't leave the hotel room in the middle of this amazing place, and everybody was upset.
We had some nice times on the trip, but I remember this one afternoon that was just terrible.
Luckily I had the sense not to act on my grumpy thoughts.
We just kept going, and it worked out in a way.
I didn't hop on the next plane and get a divorce or something like that.
I don't know if that was wisdom born of experience, or just that I'm too thick to think of doing anything like that.
Men are emotionally slow.
It's like slow motion in the emotional life of most men.
But it was a tough moment, and that was to be seen.
Later we figured out that it was the beginning of Janet coming down with a chronic fatigue type ailment, still undiagnosed to this day and still continuing to this day.
The pattern wasn't clear yet then, but patterns really aren't clear at the time.
Patterns are something we ascribe to the past and probably don't have much actual reality to them.
So we got back home, and I set about little by little just leaning into this challenging period of time.
And working.
And working harder.
We still didn't quite get it that Janet was sick, but she already had an interest in not working for a while and writing stories.
She wanted to be a writer.
So we agreed that I would work full-time and bring in all the money, and she would write.
But pretty much as soon as we got that established, it became clear there was something wrong, and she wasn't able to write very much.
And here I was working full-time, or more.

Walker was growing fast and needing all the things that three-year-olds and four-year-olds and five-year-olds need, and I was working, working, working, taking care of everything in the house, Walker.
People helped us for sure, but I was working, working, working in the middle.
And I think I was essentially a high-functioning stressaholic.
I think that's basically the case.
I was getting it all done, pretty much.
I was staying upright.
I wasn't exercising quite enough, but I was exercising some.
I wasn't sleeping quite enough, but I was sleeping at night.
I wasn't getting sick all the time or anything like that.
I was getting things done.
I was surviving.
Many good things were happening.
Really, a wonderful relationship and a wonderful family and an amazing sangha, and the sangha was growing, and all these things were great, and yet not great.
But I don't think I could really feel the ways in which they were not great.
I was just getting things done.
I was just taking care of things.
And I was little by little losing the thread of what I need.
I was putting out too much and not taking much in.
Getting support, sure.
I'm not an idiot.
We had people help us, and we eventually hired a house cleaner.
We're not totally dumb about it, but in some deep way, I was not really letting nourishment and support in.

For example, I came to practice and spirituality largely because of nature, largely because of some really important feelings I had when I was in nature, in the wilderness especially, where I used to go for weeks at a time.
And I could count on one hand how many times I'd been out in nature in the last seven years.
Well, recently I went a couple of times, so I'm up to two hands, I think.
But I did not do something that I know is important to nursing me, because I didn't have time or I didn't think about it.
Then to top it all off, two years ago, almost exactly to this day, a woman came to see me after a class and offered me $100,000 to start a new Dharma center.
That basically knocked my socks off and got me working again, if I'd ever paused, got me working harder.

It wasn't just me, it was the whole sangha, but I was somehow in the middle of the storm doing what I'm so good at, to my own detriment in many ways: taking care of business, being in the middle, keeping things moving, helping other people.
We went through all that, and if you weren't around, you can read about it.
There's a lot of stuff on the website in the newsletter section.
We went through all this and we got this building, which I'm very grateful for.
But then the final kicker that helped me realize what was happening and really helped me wake up to the situation and to return to a new chapter was that things got really awful at work.
This was really helpful, and I'm really grateful for that, actually.
I was thinking about the turn of phrase we have, "a blessing in disguise," which I guess is accurate in my case here.
The last three or four months, my work started getting really difficult and unpleasant.
But I think "a blessing in disguise" masks some limited views that are not helpful.
It suggests a dualistic assumption that the world is actually full of exactly two categories of experience.
There are blessings and there are curses.
There's good luck and there's bad luck.
There are so many ways, I think, that our language and the way we talk about our experience walls us off from the richness and the continuity and the complexity of our actual experience.
Sometimes in Zen, not here so much, but sometimes, we talk a lot about dualistic thinking.
Dualistic thinking is bad.
It can become kind of trite, but it's still an important point that we could do well to pay more attention to.
What are the many ways in which we're always dividing things into two camps, better and worse?
Left and right, more and less.
Does that really describe what's going on?
We certainly think that way about our work.
This is good, this is bad.
I like this about it, I don't like that about it.
Blessings and curses.
So anyway, my job was becoming more and more chaotic and corporate and confused.
I became the lead on a project that was clearly not going to end well no matter how hard I worked, because of earlier choices that had been made.
This led to many more phone conferences and crises and weekend calls and so on.
I was pretty good at it.

I was working, working, working, trying to take care of everything and everybody and like the other people, but it was clearly a no-win situation and very stressful, and it was really making me upset.
And then, in the middle of the worst economic downturn since who knows when, I was starting to think out loud about quitting a really high-paid, stable job.
It's interesting, too: I mentioned that to a few people who said to me, "Oh, you must be so lucky to have that job."
And I said, "Oh yeah, you're right, right, right!
I'm lucky to have this job."
But I wasn't lucky to have that job.
The job was really miserable and stressing me out and had gotten under my skin.
Finally it dawned on me that there were some serious signs of stress, some evidence, and that maybe I needed to pay attention to these things and not just to my opinions and my own inner dialogue.
I was gaining weight, which is very strange for me.
I've been a skinny boy all my life.
I had a lot of anxiety, a lot of fatigue.
I was even starting to drink some alcohol, which is unusual for me, like two beers a week or something, but it surprised me once I thought about it, the desire for that arising.
And I was finding myself pretty grumpy with my son, with Walker.
That last one was important for me to notice.
That was really kind of a shocker.
If I can't be present and happy with my seven-year-old beautiful boy, what am I doing?
What could be more important than that?

So I finally figured out I had to reach out in a more deliberate way, and not just mention to people, "Oh, I'm really stressed out at work, but it's a great job, blah, blah, blah," so they can say, "Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah."
I got some helpful advice from people.
I really sat down with them and made phone calls and asked them to please listen to me and help me.
That was really helpful, because that's another thing I think we do so strongly.
We really, all of us, think that it's just up to us.
It's my job to figure out my life.
It's my problem.
It was my decision.
These are my choices.
I have to sort this out.
But actually, of course, we all need help.
When I allowed myself to get some more help, I started to realize the many ways that I was not listening to all kinds of good advice I'd been getting all along.
I had surrounded myself with loving others, but I was still going it alone.
I was putting the world on my shoulder, and I was able to hold it there pretty well.
"Thank you very much, so I don't really need any help."
So I got some good support there, and, of course, always from my wife.
Then, sort of out of nowhere, a pretty good freelance contract arrived, which gave me courage.
Well, maybe I would be okay to leave this job.
Maybe the world won't end.
That helped set me up.
Then I was really trying to notice what my barriers were.

Once I had actually introduced the idea of making a change, and it's interesting how there are certain changes that are off limits to us in our minds at times, the idea of leaving this job was completely off limits for quite a while in my mind.
That thought couldn't really happen.
But once that thought could happen, then it was possible to study: well, what's preventing that?
What's holding me back?
What's arising?
What I noticed was a very strong fear, a very tight, gnawing, debilitating fear.
I looked at it, and I noticed eventually that it wasn't the fear of economic trouble.
It wasn't a fear of running out of money or economic worries with my family.
I somehow have faith that money will always work out.
It was a strong fear of disappointing others.
As I looked at that, I realized it was like all others.
All others that could exist, I didn't want to disappoint.
I noticed a great fear of disappointing my boss at Ernst & Young, who I've met in person about twice and talked to maybe ten times.
I didn't want to disappoint her.
Nice person.
I didn't want to disappoint my coworkers.
I didn't want to disappoint my boss at the local consulting company that got me to this job, this contract.
And then even a great fear of disappointing my mother popped up, very visually.
I was trying to look at this fear, and then suddenly this image of my mom's face just popped up.
And I thought, what are you doing here?
Hi.
So I finally worked through that enough that I thought, okay, well, it's hard, but I'm going to make this call.
I procrastinated a few days, and I thought, well, I've got to give notice because I've got to start this other thing.
I have to do this.
Then Buddha sent me some encouragement.
This is a fun story to tell.
Maybe I told a few of you this story already.
I finally psyched myself up to call my boss at Ernst & Young, make this terrible call, and ruin her day.
I was sure I was going to ruin her day.
I'm literally reaching for the office phone, and then the home phone rings.
At that moment, I'm reaching and the home phone rings.
Janet usually answers that phone.
When I'm working, it's usually play dates or her mom or friends wanting to coordinate with us.
But she was out, so I went ahead and picked up the home phone.
It wasn't about play dates.
It was an old client of mine from about seven years ago.
I probably hadn't talked to this man in six years maybe.
From before this chapter, when I was freelancing before, I built some software for his company.
It was a pretty large project at the time.
He was calling, seemingly out of the blue, to see if I would be available for a totally new software project, a significant large project, and could I start right away?
It turned out over further negotiations that he'd be willing to pay me a very high consulting rate to do this project.
For a little while anyway, I'd be making more than I was making at Ernst & Young, at my incredible, perfect, objectively perfect but miserable job.
So that was kind of interesting.
I told him, "Hold on, I've got to give notice," and made the call.
"I'll call you back."
So maybe, who knows?

I'm not a great believer in the magic of the universe, but it could be that when we make a difficult decision, make a choice that is really right for our hearts, there is some response from the universe.
Who knows?
I don't want to promise anything.
If you're thinking about doing something dramatic, you never know what's going to happen.
The other thing I realized that held me in a situation that really wasn't right for me was a great desire for things to make sense.
You know what I mean?
This was another issue besides disappointing others, another sort of fear: a fear of being someone who doesn't make sense.
Why would it make sense to my coworkers who were staying on that job that I was wanting to leave?
If I was saying, "Well, this job is really stressful and difficult," and someone right next to me is able to do the job, why would that make sense?
It doesn't make any sense.
If they're basically doing okay, how could I not be doing okay?
Which means there's something wrong with me.
We want things to make sense, and we also expect that given the same apparent external conditions, all people should experience the same thing.
Don't you think we think that way?
If I hold up this bell striker, I think you're all seeing the exact same bell striker.
Whether that's true or not is debatable, but we think that way, right?
And we think that way about our internal life as well.
So I think sense-making really got in my way, and I think that's an important thing for us to study.
What are the ways in which we're limiting our life by trying to make sense and trying to be someone who makes sense?
Can we instead just report to people in our life what we're actually experiencing?
What's true for us, without apology, without pre-verification, if we're on that side of things, or without righteousness and indignation if we're on that side?
It's two halves of the same thing.
And are we doing these maneuvers to cover for our fear of being that one who doesn't make sense?
Being the one who doesn't make sense is probably also the one who won't fit in, who won't be liked, who won't be one of us.
So that's probably a lot more detailed than you needed to know about my story, but I thought you'd enjoy it.
The important point is our journey to actually feel what we're really feeling and learn how to really take care of ourselves deeply.
How do we take care of ourselves?
Well, it does not seem to work to try to take care of yourself by walling yourself off and trying to make yourself into something that you're not.
Sometimes taking care of ourselves sounds like: if only I could pull myself out, that would be taking care of myself.
If only I could take a real break.
If only I could take a year off.
If only I could do this or do that.
The other side of stress that was kind of interesting in the last four months is that I had various escape fantasies, which evolved out of this feeling of pulling myself out.
If I could just pull myself out of my life, I'd be okay.
The main one was that I convinced myself for a couple of weeks that I should absolutely go and get a PhD in Buddhist studies.
That would really be good and it would really solve everything.
Maybe not, but I was convinced.
I did a lot of research.
I can tell you a lot about the current state of Buddhist studies in American universities right now, if you want to know.
I even visited one, actually.
So anyway, two.
So anyway, how can we really take care of ourselves?
It doesn't seem to be that our conventional idea of just taking a deep break is actually taking care of ourselves.
Pulling off to the side somewhere where we could repair the damage, sort of oil ourselves up before we re-enter the madness.

I think I'm seeing more and more that taking care of ourselves is more like fully engaging in the world with more honesty, less self-deception, less needing to make sense or explain ourselves, more willingness to just hang out there and merge and interact deeply with others.
That we take care of ourselves in cooperation with the whole world.

That the minute we convince ourselves again of our separateness and believe so strongly in that separate individual self that has to take care of itself and protect itself and avoid trouble, then we can't take care of ourselves.

And in my case, it seems like by turning finally towards my experience with more honesty and really feeling what I was actually feeling and relating to my work world with more honesty, even if it didn't make sense, I was able to initiate a change which the universe responded to, strangely enough.
And I instantly felt a lot better and am continuing little by little to feel a lot better, to feel more content and happy in my life.
It's like, you know the expression "weight lifted"?
It's like a weight is slowly lifting.
It feels that way.
And then in Buddhism we have these vows.
We have these vows of the Bodhisattva to be of service to others, to save all beings.
Except it doesn't say others.
We just think it's others, because that's our habit: that we are the one over here who's going to save those beings over there.
And so we have to get strong and get enlightened and go to therapy so we're emotionally good and get ready to reach out and save those other beings over there.
And that's really hard work.
It's really hard work trying to save beings in that way.
And so I'm reporting back that I tried that out for seven years and it's really exhausting.
There are apparently good results sometimes, but the subtle result is not too good.
I've studied for those seven years, or three sets of seven years now, 21 years, I've studied these teachings of Buddhism.
One of the central teachings is speaking exactly to this point: that this idea of the separate self is a mirage, is a dream.
It's something we impute on top of our experience.
In particular, I've studied the Diamond Sutra several times and even gave classes on the Diamond Sutra, and it makes that point over and over and over again in a million different ways.
It's like a dialogue between the Buddha and his disciple Sibuti.
He says over and over things like:
*Beings, Sibuti, beings are said by the Tathagata, the Buddha, to not be beings, to be no beings.
Thus they are called beings.
And thus does the Tathagata say all beings have no self, all beings have no individuality, all beings have no soul.*
In other words, a long polemic trying to short-circuit that habit of thinking of separateness, of individuality, of solidity, of self.
There is a self, apparently, but it's not so solid in that way.
And so I had studied these teachings for 21 years, but it took seven years of trying too hard for it to sink in a little more.
And that's the thing I think about Dharma or any spiritual practice.
It's really about understanding human life as a lived experience.
And so teachings can be like seeds, maybe.
We can plant them and cultivate them and maybe one day they'll sprout.
But just reading sutras and wise words doesn't really change anything.
We have to go through the living of the teachings and the experience of our life and learn through that.
We have to suffer a little, maybe for seven years, to understand a point.
And once you understand a little more the emptiness of self and other, which I don't know if I do yet, maybe another seven years, but a little more.
Once we understand the lack of solidity, the softness of those boundaries, the deep interaction of our living, and it comes and goes.
But as this sinks into our bones, we can lighten up a little bit.
It's not all on you, because there's not a you there for it to be on.
And I definitely still have all my habits of mind.
I have my proud inheritance from my father, my father's father, to work too hard, take things just a little bit too seriously, but at the same time I've lightened up.
I'm trying to feel my life more fully and feel more joy and contentment.
And that song, which I'll play for you one day, somehow expresses that feeling.
But like anything, it's something we have to practice with, I have to practice with, I have to remember, I have to touch again and again, open to it.
Right now I have a very flexible, low-stress work contract, it's enough, I don't have to do it full time either.
But I have to notice, I can still get sucked in, I can still work too hard, unnecessarily.
I did a little bit of that yesterday.
Today, much better.
And so I've really gotten interested in these questions.
These questions are on energy, ambition, attachment, and our powerful desire to make sense, and the way that sense-making can cloud our vision.
And I especially recommend the study of energy, actually.
This is a very concrete, straightforward thing you can do.
Really try to notice the effects on your energy.
You can feel whether you feel energetic, right?
Notice the effects on your energy of different actions and choices of body, speech, and mind.
And try to notice how it actually goes, not how you think it's supposed to go, or how you think it usually goes, or how it always is for you, but notice how it actually goes.
Like I notice that my energy is massively deflated if I complain to myself.
I instantly have less energy if I indulge in complaining, and complaining can be very subtle, you know?
It can be just a little... a little complaint about some little ache or pain or thing you don't like.
And complaining really diminishes my energy.
That's what I notice.
You can see for you.
And there are many other things like that.
Zazen practice with the sangha almost always increases my energy, even times I don't feel like doing it.
Notice that.
Pretty consistently for 21 years.
And in addition to all this heady and interesting inner psychological stuff, I've also become interested in the new and incredible power of just simple mindfulness.
Simple mindfulness of the present moment.
The healing power of returning to the breath in the body.
And I've been doing this for some time.
Pretty much throughout my seven-year chapter, I've kept up with zazen practice almost every day.
I sat in the morning at home.
Not for a long time, 20, 30 minutes.
Most every morning.
I've gone to a sesshin or two every year and several shorter retreats.
And this would have been the background of my living.
But now I'm really seeing that my practice was also constricted and limited by the tightness of my understanding and my belief in my separate existence.
Which is fine.
It's just how it goes.
Our inner experience is always conditioned by how we think about things, how we perceive things, how we understand things, by our understanding.
And yet, the unconditioned always leaks in.
And there's always benefit from practice.
From making any space at all, there's always some benefit.
But I really had a deep experience of meditation the other day.
Like the most beautiful sense of how powerful and so simple this is, and how incredibly healing it is.
Not here, but at the Christian church camp.
Samish Island, which is run by a Christian group, the Community of Christ, is a place where we go every year to do retreats, as you probably know.
And they had a big reunion, you probably heard, anniversary celebration.
So Jeff and I and a few people from the Mims group went down to celebrate with them and give them a gift.
Which they love, by the way.
Did I tell you about that?
We gave them a prayer wheel, which they really appreciate.
They were just all over it.
It's wonderful.
But also, they asked me to teach them meditation.
It was really wonderful.
And it felt like such a completing of a circle for me, because our retreat there is pretty powerful.
We go every year and have for, I don't know how long now, 12 or 13 years.
I really associate being in that place with really practicing deeply.
And yet the Community of Christ guys are always mowing the lawn and cooking in the outskirts.
Practicing, in their way, for sure.
But it was really wonderful to actually get to practice with them.
It was great.
But anyway, I did very simple practice with them.
I didn't talk about Buddhism or Buddha or any of this stuff.
We just did some stretching to reconnect with our body.
We felt our breathing.
We really slowed down and tried to feel the feeling of being alive.
And we did sitting meditation and walking meditation for not very long, 15 minutes each, maybe.
And I was really moved.
It was so beautiful.
It was such a wonderful reminder of what's always available to us.
We're always breathing and embodied.
And our brains are so clever and complicated.
We think we need all kinds of things for our happiness.
We think we have to figure stuff out and figure out our seven-year chapters and our work life and all this stuff.
And then we can give Dharma talks on it.
But actually, all we need to do is breathe.
Actually, all we need to do is feel our body and appreciate the miracle.
It really is a miracle.
No matter what our condition, it really is a miracle being alive.
And Nancy and I did a similar thing with some patients who have multiple sclerosis.
And the same kind of thing, although we didn't have quite as much time.
But it's the same kind of feeling: that even if your body is stricken by some kind of terrible, objectively terrible chronic disease or degenerative disease like MS, it's still a miracle.
It's still a miracle to be alive.
